title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 10: Tañada v. Angara: The Advent of Globalization in the Philippines
keywords: Declaration of Principles and State Policies
burden of proof / burden of evidence
Uruguay Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Tañada v. Angara, the unanimous decision he penned upholding the Senate's concurrence in the WTO Agreement and, with it, the advent of globalization in the Philippines.

His framing of the century: the collapse of Fascism, Nazism and Stalinism and the last gasps of colonialism left a single superpower and a Pax Americana, so that the arena for world preeminence shifted from brute force to economic and intellectual dominance, and from government control and ownership to deregulation, privatization, globalization and liberalization institutionalized in the WTO.

The five holdings: that the Court had jurisdiction under Rule 65 to test the Senate's act for grave abuse of discretion; that the Constitution's economic nationalism provisions are non-self-executing guides that do not mandate isolationism; that treaty obligations do not impair Congress's power to legislate, since sovereignty is limited by membership in the family of nations and by pacta sunt servanda; that the TRIPS presumption shifts only the burden of evidence, not the burden of proof; and that concurrence in the WTO Agreement alone matched exactly what the Final Act required.

The Epilogue's careful separation of legality from wisdom -- the Court did not endorse the new economic paradigms, and even members who might prefer to strike down Senate Resolution 97 could not call the Senate's deliberate and overwhelming consent grave abuse -- ending with Naisbitt's Asian Renaissance and the instruction to let the people, through their elected officers, make their free choice.
sub_topics: He opened with the century-long struggle between colonialism and totalitarianism and the spirit of independence, noting the collapse of the banal totalitarianisms and the return of Hongkong and Macau to their mother states.
He observed that military and political control of geographies had become obsolete, the Cold War and the balance of nuclear terror had ended, and only one superpower remained.

He described the shift in attention from government control to deregulation, from government ownership to privatization, and from national sovereignty to globalization and liberalization, institutionalized in the WTO.

He recorded the Philippines' entry as initiated by the Ramos government to improve access to foreign markets through reduced tariffs on exports, with Senate concurrence by Resolution No. 97 and the signing of the Instrument of Ratification.

He recounted that within days Senators Tañada and Coseteng, Representatives Andolana and Arroyo and others petitioned the Supreme Court to challenge the constitutionality of Philippine adherence, and listed the five main issues.

On jurisdiction the Decision held that where a legislative act is seriously alleged to have infringed the Constitution it becomes the duty of the judiciary to settle the dispute, certiorari, prohibition and mandamus being appropriate remedies for constitutional issues.

It stressed at the same time that the Court would not review the wisdom of enlisting in the WTO, nor pass on trade liberalization as policy, nor rule on tariff reduction, but only determine whether the Senate gravely abused its discretion.

On economic nationalism it held the Article II Declaration of Principles and State Policies not self-executing but merely guides, denying a cause of action for infringement of broad principles on grounds of due process and of the lack of judicial authority to wade into social and economic policymaking.

It read the nationalism provisions together with other constitutional pronouncements: the Constitution has a bias for Filipino goods, services, labor and enterprises, yet recognizes business exchange on the bases of equality and reciprocity and limits protection to unfair foreign competition.

Answering the claim that the Charter never contemplated a borderless world of business, he compared the 1935 Constitution and the UN Charter and wrote that constitutions must be interpreted to cover future and unknown circumstances.

On legislative power it held that sovereignty, absolute on the domestic level, is subject to restrictions voluntarily accepted as a member of the family of nations, that by the doctrine of incorporation generally accepted principles of international law are part of the law of the land, and that pacta sunt servanda obliges a state to modify its legislation to fulfil its obligations.

It added that treaties by their nature limit the absoluteness of sovereignty, nations surrendering some state power for greater benefits, and quoted John F. Kennedy that the age of self-sufficient nationalism is over and the age of interdependence is here.

On judicial power it explained that the disputable presumption under Article 34 of the TRIPS provisions places on the alleged infringer only a burden of evidence, while the patent owner retains the burden of proof of identity and newness or substantial likelihood.

On the Final Act it explained that a protocol de cloture merely records the winding up of a diplomatic conference, is not the treaty itself, and required only that signatories submit the WTO Agreement for approval and adopt the Ministerial Declarations -- exactly what Senate Resolution 97 did.

In the Epilogue he acknowledged that broad principles require an independent national economy and preference for Filipino labor and products, but noted they are not themselves sources of causes of action and are balanced by mandates for a trade policy serving the general welfare on the basis of equality and reciprocity.

He concluded that the Senate's deliberate, voluntary and overwhelming consent was a legitimate exercise of sovereign duty showing no patent and gross arbitrariness, that to strike it down for policy reasons would itself be grave abuse of judicial power, and that whether the nation should join the march toward liberalization is for the people and their elected policy makers -- the WTO Agreement itself allowing withdrawal.

He closed with Naisbitt's prediction of an Asian Renaissance with the free market as catalyst, the 31 countries then negotiating for membership, and the judgment that the alternative to the WTO is isolation and stagnation.

notable_anecdotes: He noted that the ink on the ratification documents had barely dried when Senators Tañada and Coseteng, Representatives Andolana and Arroyo and several others filed their Petition on December 29, 1994, and that this was how Tañada v. Angara was born.
He remarked in the ponencia on the ferocity and passion with which the petitioners pressed their sovereignty argument, which the Court noted and appreciated before rejecting it.
He pointed out that the Final Act of the Uruguay Round, whose omission the petitioners made much of, is contained in just one page within the 36-volume record of the negotiations.
He recalled that he penned the Decision and that it was concurred in by the fourteen other justices.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Tañada v. Angara, the unanimous decision CJP penned upholding Philippine membership in the World Trade Organization. He opened with a survey of the century -- the collapse of Fascism, Nazism and Stalinism, the last gasps of colonialism, the end of the Cold War and the emergence of a single superpower -- and argued that the arena for world preeminence had shifted from brute force to economic and intellectual dominance, with attention moving from government control to deregulation, from government ownership to privatization, and from national sovereignty to globalization and liberalization, all institutionalized in the WTO the Ramos government joined to widen market access for Philippine exports. Days after the Senate concurred through Resolution No. 97, Senators Tañada and Coseteng, Representatives Andolana and Arroyo and others challenged the adherence, raising five issues. The Court held that it had jurisdiction, since a legislative act seriously alleged to infringe the Constitution makes it the judiciary's duty to settle the dispute, while stressing that it would not review the wisdom of joining or the merits of trade liberalization. It held that the Article II Declaration of Principles is not self-executing and creates no cause of action, that the Constitution favors Filipino goods and labor yet permits exchange on the bases of equality and reciprocity and never intended an isolationist policy, and that charters must be interpreted to cover future and unknown circumstances, as the 1935 Constitution's silence on the United Nations showed. It held that treaty obligations do not impair legislative power, since sovereignty is restricted by membership in the family of nations and by pacta sunt servanda; that the TRIPS presumption shifts only the burden of evidence; and that concurrence in the WTO Agreement alone conformed exactly to what the one-page Final Act required. Its Epilogue found no patent and gross arbitrariness in the Senate's overwhelming consent, warned that striking it down on policy grounds would itself be grave abuse, and left the choice to the people through their elected officers.
